class="RichText__Container-sc-39eba4fb-0 dtciDL"><p>The ability to make changes to lyrics depends largely on your IQ and your role as a Genius user.</p>

<p><strong>IQ Milestones:</strong></p>

<ul>
<li>100 IQ: You can add a song & start a thread</li>
<li>150 IQ: You’ll be able to post in the forums.</li>
<li>300 IQ: You can edit unlocked metadata & your upvotes will be counted as double (+4 instead of +2).</li>
<li>600 IQ: You’ll be able to annotate on locked songs.</li>
<li>3,000 IQ: Edit a lyric with more than 5,000 page views</li>
</ul>


<p>If a song’s lyrics are locked, only transcribers, editors, moderators, and administrators can edit them. In this type of event, contributors can make lyric suggestions, but they must be approved by a transcriber, editor, moderator, or administrator.</p></div></div></div><div class="RichText__Container-sc-39eba4fb-0 hsPRhI"><p>This guide explains all the details of our collaborative knowledge project.</p>

<p>It’s intended as a manual for new users, and a reference tool for scholars looking to better understand all aspects of Genius, including our tips on writing good annotations…</p>

<p><strong>The 10 Annotation Commandments:</strong><br>
<small><em>Follow these rules of thumb to avoid having your annotation rejected by an editor.</em></small></p>

<ol>
<li>
<strong>Don’t Restate The Lyric:</strong> Most lyrics don’t need to be <em>explained</em>—the meaning is obvious. Don’t just paraphrase them using other words! Not <em>all</em> lines need to be annotated.</li>
<li>
<strong>Write Like A Human:</strong> An annotation shouldn’t sound like a robot wrote it. Avoid overly complicated words, but don’t be too casual either.</li>
<li>
<strong>Watch Grammar & Spelling:</strong> Writing like a human doesn’t mean forgetting the basic elements of style. Annotations are important, so don’t undermine them with sloppy writing.</li>
<li>
<strong>Do Research & Hyperlink Sources:</strong> Avoid plagiarism and speculation by searching for original sources and putting the information in your own words. Don’t just cite or copy from Wikipedia. Be sure to link your sources in the annotation.</li>
<li>
<strong>Highlight All Relevant Lyrics:</strong> Don’t just highlight a single word—annotate at least one full line. Sometimes you need two or even four bars to get the full context, but be wary of highlighting more than four lines for an annotation.</li>
<li>
<strong>Master Formatting:</strong> Familiarize yourself with <a href="https://genius.com/Genius-formatting-and-markdown-guide-annotated" rel="noopener" data-api_path="/songs/193447">markdown</a>, the basic code used in annotations that allows you to create italics, bold, blockquotes, and all the other formatting flourishes that will make your ’tates a joy to read.</li>
<li>
<strong>Include Media That Adds Depth:</strong> If you add an image, it should really illustrate something <em>specific</em> in the lyric, not just a general idea.</li>
<li>
<strong>Be Objective:</strong> Your annotations shouldn’t be rude or demeaning to the artist, and you shouldn’t write like a corny superfan.</li>
<li>
<strong>Be Concise:</strong> Here’s a good challenge: say what you mean in the fewest words possible. Wordiness ruins good annotations, but don’t go overboard—not providing enough information ruins tates, too. Annotations should have more than 50 characters.</li>
<li>
<strong>Be Evergreen:</strong> Avoid time-sensitive phrasing that will quickly become inaccurate (e.g. “two years ago,” “next summer,” “recently,” “upcoming,” etc).</li>
</ol>

of thumb to avoid having your annotation rejected by an editor.\\n\\n\\n\\nDon’t Restate The Lyric: Most lyrics don’t need to be explained—the meaning is obvious. Don’t just paraphrase them using other words! Not all lines need to be annotated.\\n\\nWrite Like A Human: An annotation shouldn’t sound like a robot wrote it. Avoid overly complicated words, but don’t be too casual either.\\n\\nWatch Grammar & Spelling: Writing like a human doesn’t mean forgetting the basic elements of style. Annotations are important, so don’t undermine them with sloppy writing.\\n\\nDo Research & Hyperlink Sources: Avoid plagiarism and speculation by searching for original sources and putting the information in your own words. Don’t just cite or copy from Wikipedia. Be sure to link your sources in the annotation.\\n\\nHighlight All Relevant Lyrics: Don’t just highlight a single word—annotate at least one full line. Sometimes you need two or even four bars to get the full context, but be wary of highlighting more than four lines for an annotation.\\n\\nMaster Formatting: Familiarize yourself with markdown, the basic code used in annotations that allows you to create italics, bold, blockquotes, and all the other formatting flourishes that will make your ’tates a joy to read.\\n\\nInclude Media That Adds Depth: If you add an image, it should really illustrate something specific in the lyric, not just a general idea.\\n\\nBe Objective: Your annotations shouldn’t be rude or demeaning to the artist, and you shouldn’t write like a corny superfan.\\n\\nBe Concise: Here’s a good challenge: say what you mean in the fewest words possible. Annotations should have more than 50 characters.\\n\\nBe Evergreen: Avoid time-sensitive phrasing that will quickly become inaccurate (e.g. “two years ago,” “next summer,” “recently,” “upcoming,” etc).\\n\\n\\n\\nClick here for more on writing annotations.\",\"description\":{\"markdown\":\"This guide explains all the details of our collaborative knowledge project.\\n\\nIt\'s intended as a manual for new users, and a reference tool for scholars looking to better understand all aspects of Genius, including our tips on writing good annotations...\\n\\n**The 10 Annotation Commandments:**\\n<Small>*Follow these rules of thumb to avoid having your annotation rejected by an editor.*<\/small>\\n\\n1. **Don\'t Restate The Lyric:** Most lyrics don\'t need to be *explained*—the meaning is obvious. Don\'t just paraphrase them using other words! Not *all* lines need to be annotated.\\n2. **Write Like A Human:** An annotation shouldn\'t sound like a robot wrote it. Avoid overly complicated words, but don\'t be too casual either.\\n3. **Watch Grammar & Spelling:** Writing like a human doesn\'t mean forgetting the basic elements of style. Annotations are important, so don\'t undermine them with sloppy writing.\\n4. **Do Research & Hyperlink Sources:** Avoid plagiarism and speculation by searching for original sources and putting the information in your own words. Don\'t just cite or copy from Wikipedia. Be sure to link your sources in the annotation.\\n5. **Highlight All Relevant Lyrics:** Don\'t just highlight a single word---annotate at least one full line. Sometimes you need two or even four bars to get the full context, but be wary of highlighting more than four lines for an annotation.\\n6. **Master Formatting:** Familiarize yourself with [markdown](http://genius.com/Genius-formatting-and-markdown-guide-annotated), the basic code used in annotations that allows you to create italics, bold, blockquotes, and all the other formatting flourishes that will make your ’tates a joy to read.\\n7. **Include Media That Adds Depth:** If you add an image, it should really illustrate something *specific* in the lyric, not just a general idea.\\n8. **Be Objective:** Your annotations shouldn’t be rude or demeaning to the artist, and you shouldn’t write like a corny superfan. \\n9. **Be Concise:** Here’s a good challenge: say what you mean in the fewest words possible. How can you get involved ? —> SIGN UP FOR A GENIUS ACCOUNT You'll get your own profile page and the ability to follow other scholars and artists. Once you have an account, you can start adding knowledge and earning Genius IQ. If you're interested in adding knowledge with any of our international communities, you can do that, too! —> More info on international communities IQ is what we call the points you earn by adding knowledge. Every scholar has a total IQ number next to their name that represents how knowledgeable they are. —> More info on IQ Annotate Lyric s: Highlight any line in a song to start an annotation. Explain what a complicated lyric means, or add other interesting context. —> More on annotations Write Artist, Song & Album Bios: Write a few paragraphs that tell the story of an artist's career, or break down the key details of a specific song or album. —> More on bios Annotate Cover Artwork: Click through artwork found on any album page to start a cover art annotation —> More on annotating cover art Add Metadata : Do you know who produced a song? What sample it uses? Where it was recorded? Add all the interesting data. —> More on metadata Transcribe Lyrics: Any scholar can add a song page. Post new lyrics when a song drops, add old songs we’re missing, or correct lyrics. —> More on transcription Make A Suggestion or Propose An Edit: Could an annotation or bio be improved? Tell us what's missing and it could get integrated. —> More on suggestions & edits Ask or Answer A Question With Q&A: Anyone can ask the Genius community a question. Want to know where a song peaked on the charts? Ask away! Know the answer and want to tell us? Let us (and the world) know. —> More on Q&A Everything on Genius is collaborative. Here's how we work together and communicate. Annotations & Edits Are Reviewed: Anyone can add knowledge, but editors determine what becomes the official "Genius Annotation." —> More on editorial review Artists Add Knowledge Too: Creators who are "Verified" can write annotations, confirm lyrics, and co-sign good annotations from scholars. —> More on Verified Artists Upvotes & Pyongs: See something good on the site? Your cosign can have a real effect on the best knowledge rising to the top. —> More on upvotes & pyongs Follow People In The Newsfeed: See what other scholars are doing on the site, and get alerts when your favorite artists write annotations. —> More on the newsfeed Transcribers, Editors & Other Advanced Roles: Dedicated scholars who make quality contributions can get additional powers and responsibilities. —> More on advanced roles Direct Message Any User: Start a private conversation with anyone on Genius any time. —> More on messages The Forums: The Genius community loves talking about music and the details of our collaborative knowledge project. Get started now! —> More on the forums International Communities: Genius is thriving all around the world in many languages. Connect with scholars in your home country. —> More on International Communities Community Policy: Genius aspires to be a place where everyone feels welcome and safe. We take abuse and harassment seriously. —> Read our full Community Policy Below is a list of resources developed by the Genius Editorial Board to help educate everyone from budding contributors to seasoned veterans on editorial best practices. If you feel like we're missing something, send @streetlights a message. It’s intended as a manual for new users, and a reference tool for scholars looking to better understand all aspects of Genius, including our tips on writing good annotations… The 10 Annotation Commandments: Follow these rules of thumb to avoid having your annotation rejected by an editor. Don’t Restate The Lyric: Most lyrics don’t need to be explained —the meaning is obvious. Don’t just paraphrase them using other words! Not all lines need to be annotated. Write Like A Human: An annotation shouldn’t sound like a robot wrote it. Avoid overly complicated words, but don’t be too casual either. Watch Grammar & Spelling: Writing like a human doesn’t mean forgetting the basic elements of style. Annotations are important, so don’t undermine them with sloppy writing. Do Research & Hyperlink Sources: Avoid plagiarism and speculation by searching for original sources and putting the information in your own words. Don’t just cite or copy from Wikipedia. Be sure to link your sources in the annotation. Highlight All Relevant Lyrics: Don’t just highlight a single word—annotate at least one full line. Sometimes you need two or even four bars to get the full context, but be wary of highlighting more than four lines for an annotation. Master Formatting: Familiarize yourself with markdown , the basic code used in annotations that allows you to create italics, bold, blockquotes, and all the other formatting flourishes that will make your ’tates a joy to read. Include Media That Adds Depth: If you add an image, it should really illustrate something specific in the lyric, not just a general idea. Be Objective: Your annotations shouldn’t be rude or demeaning to the artist, and you shouldn’t write like a corny superfan. Be Concise: Here’s a good challenge: say what you mean in the fewest words possible. Wordiness ruins good annotations, but don’t go overboard—not providing enough information ruins tates, too. Annotations should have more than 50 characters. Be Evergreen: Avoid time-sensitive phrasing that will quickly become inaccurate (e.g. “two years ago,” “next summer,” “recently,” “upcoming,” etc). Click here for more on writing annotations. Expand +991 4 9 Share Q&A Find answers to frequently asked questions about the song and explore its deeper meaning Ask a question How do I submit lyrics? Genius Answer 2 contributors Once you have over 100 IQ, you can click the “Add A Song” link at the top of the page to add lyrics to Genius. Search for the song first to make sure it’s not already on Genius! Learn more about transcription here . +291 How do you annotate repeated lyrics or separated lyrics with one annotation? Genius Answer 3 contributors When you click on an annotation, the URL will change. Copy the string of numbers at the end (such as 11315517 ), then click on the “edit lyrics” button and put the text you want to be annotated in square brackets ([]) with the number next to the closing square bracket in normal brackets (()), as shown below: Here it is zoomed in more: Note that this can only be done on the same song. An annotation cannot be present over multiple tracks. +215 How can you edit a song's lyrics? Genius Answer 4 contributors Click the “Edit Lyrics” button at the top of the song page. <\/div>\\n  \\n<\/blockquote>\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n<p>Despite whatever pain he’s experiencing, he keeps getting little flashes of hope.<\/p>\\n\\n<blockquote class=\\\"g_lyrics_tag\\\">\\n  \\n    <div <\/div>\\n  \\n<\/blockquote>\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n<p>In the second verse, Antonoff might be commenting on the pressures of being a public figure (“it’s hard being perceived”), though he’s trying to work       <h2 class="article_dek">
        <div class="
          
          
        ">
          It’s on the ‘Practical Magic 2’ soundtrack.
        </div>
      </h2>

      <div class="article_rich_text_formatting">
        <p><a href="https://genius.com/artists/Jack-antonoff" rel="noopener" data-api_path="/artists/264329">Jack Antonoff</a>’s band <a href="https://genius.com/artists/Bleachers" rel="noopener" data-api_path="/artists/158659">Bleachers</a> released their fifth album, <a href="https://genius.com/albums/Bleachers/Everyone-for-ten-minutes" rel="noopener" data-api_path="/albums/1581240"><em>everyone for ten minutes</em></a>, back in May, a couple of months before <a href="https://people.com/margaret-qualley-jack-antonoff-separate-after-nearly-3-years-of-marriage-12013758" rel="noopener">news broke</a> of the singer, songwriter, and producer’s separation from wife Margaret Qualley. Today, Bleachers are back with a new tune, <a href="https://genius.com/Bleachers-caught-myself-believing-lyrics" rel="noopener" data-api_path="/songs/14232211">“Caught Myself Believing,”</a> which comes off the soundtrack for the brand-new film <em>Practical Magic 2</em>, starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman.</p>

<p></p><div class="embedly_preview"><iframe class="apple_iframe_song_embed" src="https://embed.music.apple.com/us/song/6807438578" allow="encrypted-media *;" width="100%" height="120"></iframe></div>

<p>“It was an absolute joy to get together as a band and make a song for this soundtrack,” Antonoff said in a statement. “<em>Practical Magic</em> is such a beloved story. I’m so glad the world gets a part two, and that Bleachers gets to play a small part in it.”</p>

<p>Written and produced by Antonoff, “Caught Myself Believing” has the classic Bleachers ramshackle rock ‘n’ roll sound, complete with strings and synths. The lyrics are fairly opaque, but in the opening verse, Antonoff wrestles with the past, perhaps to the detriment of his current relationship.</p>

<blockquote class="g_lyrics_tag">
  
    <div class="referent referent--white">
      Deciphering the look that’s in your eye<br>
And the complicated rhythms of trying to get by<br>
I know it’s getting crazy<br>
Me dragging all these ghosts out of your flame<br>
Oh, tell me, is it still not safe to dream?<br>
Since I’ve been a slave to a tired swing memory<br>
I blurred out the faces and bargained with shame
    </div>
  
</blockquote>





<p>Despite whatever pain he’s experiencing, he keeps getting little flashes of hope.</p>

<blockquote class="g_lyrics_tag">
  
    <div class="referent referent--white">
      But I missed myself and I missed you more<br>
Think I saw God on your bedroom floor<br>
Where you shine on and I caught myself believing
    </div>
  
</blockquote>





<p>In the second verse, Antonoff might be commenting on the pressures of being a public figure (“it’s hard being perceived”), though he’s trying to work through whatever’s dogging him and find happiness with this other person.</p>

<blockquote class="g_lyrics_tag">
  
    <div class="referent referent--white">
      What’s the point of holding on if you can’t carry much more than you stole?<br>
And leaving it all behind it feels like it’s someone you don’t know<br>
Burning some burned out memories of torn up families<br>
In you, in you I see a war I chose to fight<br>
I believed that I’d been something to see<br>
Can’t be high, can’t be real, it’s hard being perceived<br>
And it pulled me down, and it spun me round and round
    </div>
  
</blockquote>





<p>On the final chorus, he’s ready to leave his old self behind—which of course is easier said than done.</p>

<blockquote class="g_lyrics_tag">
  
    <div class="referent referent--white">
      Oh, I’m so tired, babe, of what I’ve been before<br>
It hurts to hurt, I can’t take much more<br>
But at least I’m yours<br>
And then you kiss me hard<br>
Oh, honey, rest alone ‘cause I caught myself believing
    </div>
  
</blockquote>





<p>You can <a href="https://genius.com/Bleachers-caught-myself-believing-lyrics" rel="noopener" data-api_path="/songs/14232211">read all the lyrics to “Caught Myself Believing”</a> on Genius now.</p>

Jack Antonoff ’s band Bleachers released their fifth album, everyone for ten minutes , back in May, a couple of months before news broke of the singer, songwriter, and producer’s separation from wife Margaret Qualley. Today, Bleachers are back with a new tune, “Caught Myself Believing,” which comes off the soundtrack for the brand-new film Practical Magic 2 , starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman. “It was an absolute joy to get together as a band and make a song for this soundtrack,” Antonoff said in a statement. “ Practical Magic is such a beloved story. I’m so glad the world gets a part two, and that Bleachers gets to play a small part in it.” Written and produced by Antonoff, “Caught Myself Believing” has the classic Bleachers ramshackle rock ‘n’ roll sound, complete with strings and synths. The lyrics are fairly opaque, but in the opening verse, Antonoff wrestles with the past, perhaps to the detriment of his current relationship. Deciphering the look that’s in your eye And the complicated rhythms of trying to get by I know it’s getting crazy Me dragging all these ghosts out of your flame Oh, tell me, is it still not safe to dream? Since I’ve been a slave to a tired swing memory I blurred out the faces and bargained with shame Despite whatever pain he’s experiencing, he keeps getting little flashes of hope. But I missed myself and I missed you more Think I saw God on your bedroom floor Where you shine on and I caught myself believing In the second verse, Antonoff might be commenting on the pressures of being a public figure (“it’s hard being perceived”), though he’s trying to work through whatever’s dogging him and find happiness with this other person. What’s the point of holding on if you can’t carry much more than you stole? And leaving it all behind it feels like it’s someone you don’t know Burning some burned out memories of torn up families In you, in you I see a war I chose to fight I believed that I’d been something to see Can’t be high, can’t be real, it’s hard being perceived And it pulled me down, and it spun me round and round On the final chorus, he’s ready to leave his old self behind—which of course is easier said than done. Oh, I’m so tired, babe, of what I’ve been before It hurts to hurt, I can’t take much more But at least I’m yours And then you kiss me hard Oh, honey, rest alone ‘cause I caught myself believing You can read all the lyrics to “Caught Myself Believing” on Genius now.
